The immune response to infections includes both innate and adaptive immunity mechanisms. Innate responses involve immediate barriers like skin, inflammatory responses, and phagocytic cells. Adaptive immunity develops specific responses through T-cells and B-cells, creating antibodies and memory cells for long-term protection against future exposures.

Vaccines work by introducing antigens from pathogens into the body without causing disease, stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies and activate memory cells. This preparation allows rapid recognition and response when the actual pathogen is encountered, providing immunity through immunological memory.

The cardiovascular system is responsible for circulating blood throughout the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues while removing waste products. It consists of the heart as a pump, blood vessels as transport pathways, and blood as the transport medium for gases, nutrients, hormones, and immune cells.

DNA replication is a semiconservative process in which the double helix unwinds and each strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides in the five-prime to three-prime direction, while helicase unwinds the helix and ligase seals the fragments on the lagging strand.

Protein synthesis proceeds in two stages. Transcription copies a gene into messenger RNA inside the nucleus, and translation reads that message at the ribosome, where transfer RNAs deliver amino acids according to the genetic code to build a polypeptide chain.

Cellular respiration converts glucose into usable chemical energy. Glycolysis splits glucose in the cytoplasm, the citric acid cycle oxidises the resulting molecules in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation uses the electron transport chain to generate the bulk of the cell's ATP.

Antibiotics target structures and processes unique to bacteria, such as cell wall synthesis, ribosomal protein production, or DNA gyrase activity. Because human cells lack these targets, well-chosen antibiotics can clear a bacterial infection with limited harm to the patient.

Antibiotic resistance emerges when mutations or horizontally transferred genes allow bacteria to survive exposure to a drug. Common mechanisms include enzymatic degradation of the antibiotic, modification of the drug target, reduced membrane permeability, and active efflux pumps.

Epidemiologists study how diseases are distributed in populations and which factors influence that distribution. Core measures include incidence, prevalence, and the basic reproduction number, which together describe how quickly and widely a condition spreads.

The nervous system coordinates the body through electrical and chemical signalling. Neurons conduct action potentials along their axons and release neurotransmitters at synapses, where receptors on the receiving cell convert the chemical signal back into an electrical response.

Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy in plants and algae. Light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membranes generate ATP and NADPH, which the Calvin cycle then uses in the stroma to fix carbon dioxide into carbohydrate.

Mendelian inheritance describes how discrete alleles segregate during gamete formation and recombine at fertilisation. Dominant alleles mask recessive ones in heterozygotes, producing the characteristic phenotype ratios observed in monohybrid and dihybrid crosses.

Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower the activation energy of reactions. Their activity depends on the shape of the active site and is sensitive to temperature, pH, substrate concentration, and the presence of inhibitors or cofactors.

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external change. Negative feedback loops involving receptors, control centres, and effectors regulate variables such as body temperature, blood glucose, and osmotic balance.

The respiratory system exchanges gases between air and blood. Air travels through the trachea and bronchi into alveoli, where oxygen diffuses into capillary blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out along their partial pressure gradients.

Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells and underlies growth and tissue repair. Meiosis instead halves the chromosome number over two divisions and introduces variation through crossing over and independent assortment, producing gametes.

Clinical trials evaluate medical interventions in sequential phases. Early phases assess safety and dosing in small groups, while later randomised controlled phases compare efficacy against a control arm in larger populations under blinded conditions.

The endocrine system regulates physiology through hormones released into the bloodstream. Glands such as the thyroid, adrenal glands, and pancreas secrete signalling molecules that bind receptors on distant target cells to alter their activity.

Ecosystems transfer energy through trophic levels, from producers that capture sunlight to primary and secondary consumers and finally decomposers. Energy is lost as heat at each transfer, which limits the length of most food chains.

Molecular diagnostics detect pathogens or genetic variants by amplifying and reading nucleic acid sequences. Polymerase chain reaction, sequencing, and hybridisation assays each trade off sensitivity, specificity, turnaround time, and cost.
